### Problem: Stick Lengths {#sec-srt-p5-a}

::: {.p-statement}
$n$ sticks with lengths $p_1, \dots, p_n$ ($1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, $1 \le p_i \le 10^9$). In one move you may lengthen or shorten any stick by $1$, and each unit of change costs $1$. Make **all sticks equal** with minimum total cost, and print that cost.

Source: [CSES 1074 · Stick Lengths](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1074){.solved}

Example: `5 / 2 3 1 5 2` → $5$ (choose target $2$: costs $0+1+1+3+0=5$).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Only the *multiset* of lengths matters, so sort. For a target $t$, the cost is $f(t) = \sum_i |p_i - t|$ — a sum of absolute deviations — and @sec-srt-a5's promise is that **the median minimises it**. Exchange argument: slide $t$ one step to the right. Every stick at or left of $t$ becomes one unit more expensive, every stick right of $t$ one unit cheaper, so $f$ changes by $(\# \text{ at or left of } t) - (\# \text{ right of } t)$. While more than half the sticks sit to the right, moving right strictly helps; once at least half sit at or left of $t$, moving right never helps. The turning point is the middle element of the sorted array, $b_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}$, which is an actual stick length (for even $n$ every point between the two middle elements ties).
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Try every candidate target.** The minimiser of a sum of absolute deviations always sits *at* one of the values (between two consecutive values $f$ is linear with a fixed slope, so the turn happens at a data point). For each $t \in \{p_i\}$ compute $\sum_i |p_i - t|$ and keep the minimum. $O(n^2)$ — the oracle.
2. **Sort + prefix sums, evaluate cost at every data point in $O(1)$.** Sort $p$ into $b$; build the running sum $\mathit{pref}[k] = b_0 + \dots + b_{k-1}$. Then for target $t = b[i]$, the cost splits into left-side and right-side closed forms and evaluates in $O(1)$: $\mathit{cost}(b[i]) = b[i](i{+}1) - \mathit{pref}[i{+}1] + (\mathit{pref}[n] - \mathit{pref}[i{+}1]) - b[i](n - i - 1)$. Try every $i$, keep the min. $O(n\log n)$ total (sort dominates).
3. **Sort, take the median.** Answer $= \sum_i |b_i - b_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}|$ where $b$ is the sorted array. $O(n\log n)$ time from the sort; the scan afterwards is $O(n)$.

**Invariant.** With $t = b_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}$, at least half the sticks are $\le t$ and at least half are $\ge t$. So stepping right changes $f$ by $(\#\le t) - (\#> t) \ge 0$ and stepping left by $(\#\ge t) - (\#< t) \ge 0$; $f$ is convex (a sum of V-shaped terms), so a point where no single step helps is a global minimum.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Try every candidate target

::: {.form-next}
Test every stick length as the common target, compute the full move cost for each, and keep the best. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space — with $n$ up to $2 \cdot 10^5$ this is far too slow, which is precisely what forces the median insight; it stays as the oracle.

**Worked example.** $p = [2, 3, 1, 5, 2]$. Targets: $t=1 \Rightarrow 1+2+0+4+1=8$; $t=2 \Rightarrow 0+1+1+3+0=5$; $t=3 \Rightarrow 1+0+2+2+1=6$; $t=5 \Rightarrow 3+2+4+0+3=12$. Best is $t=2$ with cost $5$ — and $2$ is the median of the sorted list $[1,2,2,3,5]$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("stick", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "5"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def stick_brute(p):
    best = math.inf
    for t in p:
        best = min(best, sum(abs(x - t) for x in p))
    return best
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - try every value as target (O(n^2) oracle)
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
ll stickBrute(vector<ll> p) {
    ll best = (ll)4e18;
    for (ll t : p) {
        ll cost = 0;
        for (ll x : p) cost += abs(x - t);
        best = min(best, cost);
    }
    return best;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The outer loop `for t in p` only needs the *present* values: between two consecutive stick lengths, $f(t)$ is a line whose slope only changes at a data point, so a minimum is attained at some $p_i$. The inner sum $\sum |p_i - t|$ is the literal cost of gathering every stick to $t$. `best` keeps the winner. `ll` (long long) everywhere in C++ because the answer reaches $\approx 10^{14}$.

#### Sort + prefix sums, evaluate every data point in $O(1)$

::: {.form-next}
The brute force is $O(n^2)$ because each candidate target costs a full $O(n)$ rescan. Sort the array, build a running sum, and turn each candidate's cost into **one arithmetic formula** using two halves — sticks strictly to the left of the target and sticks to the right. Evaluating $f$ at every data point then takes $O(n)$ after an $O(n\log n)$ sort. Same asymptotic total as form 3, but *no median insight required* — the sort + prefix machinery answers "which target wins?" by brute enumeration over the $n$ candidates, each at $O(1)$. The next rung notices that the whole table of costs is unnecessary because the answer is always the middle index.

**Prefix sums, in plain words** (@sec-pref). $\mathit{pref}[k]$ stores $b_0 + \dots + b_{k-1}$, so any contiguous sum is one subtraction. Applied to a sorted array with target $t = b[i]$: the left side contributes $t + t + \dots + t$ ($i{+}1$ times) minus the actual sum of $b[0..i]$, and the right side is the actual sum of $b[i{+}1..n-1]$ minus $t$ times its count. Two table lookups, four multiplications, one sum.

**Worked example.** $p = [2, 3, 1, 5, 2]$ sorted $b = [1, 2, 2, 3, 5]$, $\mathit{pref} = [0, 1, 3, 5, 8, 13]$ (so $\mathit{pref}[k]$ is the sum of the first $k$ sorted values). Evaluate $f$ at each data point:

- $t = b[0] = 1$: $\mathit{lc} = 1 \cdot 1 - 1 = 0$; $\mathit{rc} = (13 - 1) - 1 \cdot 4 = 8$; cost $8$.
- $t = b[1] = 2$: $\mathit{lc} = 2 \cdot 2 - 3 = 1$; $\mathit{rc} = (13 - 3) - 2 \cdot 3 = 7$; cost $8$.
- $t = b[2] = 2$: $\mathit{lc} = 2 \cdot 3 - 5 = 1$; $\mathit{rc} = (13 - 5) - 2 \cdot 2 = 4$; cost $5$.
- $t = b[3] = 3$: $\mathit{lc} = 3 \cdot 4 - 8 = 4$; $\mathit{rc} = (13 - 8) - 3 \cdot 1 = 2$; cost $6$.
- $t = b[4] = 5$: $\mathit{lc} = 5 \cdot 5 - 13 = 12$; $\mathit{rc} = 0$; cost $12$.

Best $= 5$, at $t = b[2] = 2$ — which is exactly the middle index, telling you the next rung can skip every row but that one.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p_):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("stick", "prefix")
    assert str(final) == "5"
    V.story(ax, p_, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-1074-prefix
def stick_prefix(p):
    b = sorted(p)
    n = len(b)
    pref = [0]
    for x in b:
        pref.append(pref[-1] + x)          # pref[k] = b[0] + ... + b[k-1]
    best = math.inf
    for i in range(n):
        t = b[i]
        lc = t * (i + 1) - pref[i + 1]                       # sum |x - t| for x in b[0..i]
        rc = (pref[n] - pref[i + 1]) - t * (n - i - 1)       # sum |x - t| for x in b[i+1..n-1]
        best = min(best, lc + rc)
    return best

for _ in range(300):
    p = [random.randint(1, 40) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 10))]
    assert stick_prefix(p) == stick_brute(p)
assert stick_prefix([2, 3, 1, 5, 2]) == 5
print("stick_prefix OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
using ll = long long;

ll stickPrefix(vector<ll> p) {
    sort(p.begin(), p.end());
    int n = (int)p.size();
    vector<ll> pref(n + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) pref[i + 1] = pref[i] + p[i];
    ll best = (ll)4e18;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        ll t = p[i];
        ll lc = t * (i + 1) - pref[i + 1];
        ll rc = (pref[n] - pref[i + 1]) - t * (n - i - 1);
        best = min(best, lc + rc);
    }
    return best;
}

int main() { vector<ll> v{2, 3, 1, 5, 2}; cout << stickPrefix(v) << '\n'; }
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `pref.append(pref[-1] + x)` builds the running-sum table over the sorted copy. `t * (i + 1) - pref[i + 1]` is the *left* deviation: at target $t = b[i]$, every stick $b[0..i]$ costs $t - b[j]$, which sums to $(i+1) t - (b[0] + \dots + b[i]) = (i+1) t - \mathit{pref}[i+1]$. `rc` mirrors it on the right: $(b[i+1] + \dots + b[n-1]) - t(n - i - 1) = (\mathit{pref}[n] - \mathit{pref}[i+1]) - t(n - i - 1)$. The loop over $i$ evaluates $f$ at every data point, in $O(1)$ each. Total $O(n\log n)$ for sort + table + scan — **matching form 3 in asymptotics but not in insight**: form 3 gets the answer in one lookup after the sort, whereas form 2 still walks every candidate. All arithmetic is `ll`, because each partial product $t \cdot (i+1)$ alone can reach $10^{14}$.

#### Sort, then gather at the median

::: {.form-next}
The exchange argument in one line: sort, pick the middle element as target, and sum the distances. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ or $O(1)$ extra space. This is @sec-srt-a5's theorem used verbatim — the median minimises absolute deviations. Compared to form 2, we drop the prefix table entirely and evaluate $f$ once, at $b[n/2]$.

**Why the median, in plain words.** Picture the sticks on a number line and stand at position $t$; the cost is your total distance to all of them. Step one unit toward the majority side and you come closer to more sticks than you move away from, so the cost drops. The moment strictly more than half the sticks are behind you, every further step costs net. You stop exactly when neither side has a majority — at the median.

**Worked example.** $p = [2,3,1,5,2]$ sorted $b = [1,2,2,3,5]$; median $b_{5//2} = b_2 = 2$. Cost $|1-2|+|2-2|+|2-2|+|3-2|+|5-2| = 1+0+0+1+3 = 5$ — the same target the $O(n^2)$ search and the $O(n\log n)$ prefix scan both found.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p_):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("stick", "median")
    assert str(final) == "5"
    V.story(ax, p_, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-1074-median
def stick_median(p):
    b = sorted(p)
    t = b[len(b) // 2]
    return sum(abs(x - t) for x in b)

for _ in range(300):
    p = [random.randint(1, 40) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 10))]   # odd and even n
    assert stick_median(p) == stick_brute(p)
assert stick_median([2, 3, 1, 5, 2]) == 5          # CSES example; the board sample
assert stick_median([1, 2, 9, 10]) == 16            # even n: any t in [2, 9] costs 16
assert stick_median([7]) == 0                       # single stick
assert stick_median([1, 1, 9, 9, 9]) == 16          # gather at 9: 8+8=16
print("stick_median OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
using ll = long long;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n; cin >> n;
    vector<ll> p(n);
    for (ll& x : p) cin >> x;
    sort(p.begin(), p.end());
    ll t = p[n / 2];
    ll cost = 0;
    for (ll x : p) cost += abs(x - t);
    cout << cost << '\n';
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `b = sorted(p)` puts the majority-counting argument to work: the middle element `b[len(b)//2]` has at least half the sticks at or below it and at least half at or above it, for odd and even $n$ alike (summing over the sorted copy makes no difference to the total). `sum(abs(x - t) for x in b)` is the gathering cost, and `ll`/long long is mandatory — $2 \cdot 10^5$ sticks at distance up to $10^9$ overflows `int` by five orders of magnitude. The C++ version reads the whole CSES input shape: $n$, then the lengths, one answer line.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Try every target** is $O(n^2)$ time. **Sort + prefix sums** is $O(n\log n)$ time (the sort dominates; the table and scan are $O(n)$) and $O(n)$ extra space for the prefix table — same asymptotics as the median form, but no insight into *which* data point wins is required. **Sort + median** is $O(n\log n)$ time and $O(n)$ or $O(1)$ space; the entire prefix machinery collapses once you know the median is the answer. The prize is reusable: whenever an objective is a sum of absolute deviations $\sum |x_i - t|$, the answer hides at a median — @sec-srt-p5-b weights each deviation and the same exchange argument moves the stopping point to a *weighted* median.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 1$: cost $0$ — the median is the only stick itself.
- Even $n$: the statement does not promise odd $n$. Every target between the two middle values ties (the cost curve is flat there), so `b[n // 2]` is still optimal; the even-$n$ stress tests check it.
- Answer fits in $64$ bits ($\le 10^{14}$) but **not** in `int` — the classic CSES submission failure.
:::

- [CF 1486B · Eastern Exhibition](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1486/B){rating="1500"} — the median in two dimensions, and counting *all* optimal points: the length of the flat segment.
